clinicalPearls: A benign inflammatory condition producing painful, non-suppurative swelling of the upper costal cartilages, most often the second or third
The presence of visible and palpable localised swelling distinguishes Tietze syndrome from costochondritis, which causes tenderness without swelling
Usually affects a single site and tends to occur in younger adults, in contrast to the more diffuse, multi-level costochondritis
Pain is reproduced by palpation of the affected costal cartilage and may be aggravated by coughing, deep breathing or movement
It is fundamentally a clinical diagnosis, made after excluding cardiac, pulmonary and other serious causes of chest pain
Imaging is used chiefly to exclude other pathology, though MRI or CT may show cartilage enlargement and oedema
Management is reassurance, activity modification, NSAIDs, and local corticosteroid injection for resistant cases
reference.pathophysiology: Tietze syndrome is a localised, benign inflammation of the costochondral, costosternal or sternoclavicular cartilage of unknown precise cause. Repetitive minor trauma, coughing or physical strain is thought to trigger a self-limiting inflammatory and possibly reparative response within the costal cartilage, producing cartilage enlargement with surrounding soft-tissue oedema. Unlike infective or destructive processes there is no suppuration or bony erosion; the visible fusiform swelling reflects benign cartilage and perichondrial thickening rather than joint destruction, and the condition resolves once the inflammation settles although the swelling may persist for some time.
additionalDifferentials: Rib fracture or costal cartilage injury
Anterior chest wall involvement of SAPHO syndrome or seronegative arthropathy
additionalInvestigations: ECG and cardiac assessment to exclude ischaemic chest pain
Chest radiograph to exclude pulmonary and rib pathology
MRI or CT of the chest wall to characterise cartilage swelling and exclude tumour or infection
Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) when an inflammatory or infective process is considered
Ultrasound of the affected costal cartilage to confirm localised swelling
redFlags: Chest pain with cardiac features (exertional, radiating, associated with breathlessness or diaphoresis)
Constitutional symptoms or a hard fixed mass suggesting malignancy
Fever and progressive swelling raising concern for infection
Pain unresponsive to conservative measures with atypical features
reference.prognosis: Tietze syndrome is benign and usually self-limiting, with pain settling over weeks to months, although the palpable swelling can persist for a prolonged period; recurrence is possible but serious sequelae do not occur.
pitfalls: Anchoring on a musculoskeletal cause and missing cardiac or pulmonary disease
Confusing it with costochondritis by overlooking the characteristic localised swelling
Ordering unnecessary invasive investigation for a benign self-limiting condition
Failing to consider SAPHO syndrome or malignancy when swelling is atypical or persistent
management: Reassure the patient after excluding cardiac, pulmonary and other serious causes, as the condition is benign and self-limiting
Relieve pain with simple analgesia and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, together with local heat and activity modification
Advise avoidance of aggravating movements, coughing strain and repetitive loading of the chest wall
Offer a local corticosteroid and anaesthetic injection into the affected cartilage for pain that does not settle
Explain that the palpable swelling may persist after the pain resolves and does not indicate serious disease
Re-evaluate if new or atypical features emerge that suggest an alternative diagnosis
